newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Swaziland braces for pro-democracy blockade.
newsitem.headline: Swaziland braces for pro-democracy blockade.

text.p: Landlocked Swaziland will have all its borders with South Africa and Mozambique blocked on Monday by unions from all three states demanding democracy in the southern African kingdom, unions said on Sunday.

The Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU) has waged a month-old strike, with a patchy following, to back its demands for a speedy move towards democracy, the federation secretary general Jan Sithole said.

"We are happy there will be this blockade because hopefully it will drive some sanity into the government and make them take negotiations which will start on Wednesday seriously," he told Reuters at a rally by 1,500 sugar workers in eastern Swaziland.
"We are also calling for a total strike by all workers in Swaziland tomorrow."
The mighty Congress of South African Trade Unions said on Friday it would support SFTU in its demands for greater political freedom by blocking goods moving in and out of Swaziland on Monday.
Swaziland, with a population of 900,000, is heavily reliant on South Africa, which absorbs over half its exports.
Sithole said unions in Mozambique had also agreed to block border posts which offer Swaziland access to Maputo, its closest harbour.

The union has presented the Swazi government with a list of 27 demands which include the repeal of a 1973 royal decree in which all state powers were vested in the monarchy and political parties were banned.
Swazilands's two major foreign exchange earners, the sugar and timber industries, have been hardest hit by the strike.
Sithole said there had been a 100 percent stayaway in the timber and sugar belts. The sugar industry has said it stands to lose up to $700,000 a day.
Political analysts say a lack of unity among the unions meant that other factories had largely escaped the call for a nationwide strike over the last month.
After a violent strike last year, King Mswati III set up a review commission to make recommendations on drawing up a constitutional democracy.
The commission, which has two years in which to make its findings, has irked the union federation which says it is not representative and listens only to submissions made by individuals.
